PICTURE NCA/PSNI By Hannah Patterson August 11, 2026 at 5:42pm BST A van driver who claimed he was delivering a hot tub has been jailed for smuggling cannabis. The National Crime Agency investigation found the driver was smuggling cannabis worth £220,000 into Northern Ireland and across the border to the Republic of Ireland. NCA officers arrested Lithuanian national Paulius Andrulis at Belfast port on 15 th June 2025 after he arrived on a sailing from Cairnryan port in Scotland. Border Force officers questioned the 37-year-old, with him teling them he was delivering a hot tub to an address in Mullingar in West Meath. Sinn Féin’s John Finucane won’t confirm if he met with Daniel Kinahan and compares it to asking a surgeon which patients they’d spoken to Decision to ban Drumcree parade to be quashed, High Court Judge rules When officers searched the vehicle, a purpose-built hide was discovered in the roof containing 27.5 kilos of herbal cannabis, a class B drug. The hide ran the length of the roof of the van, with access through the top of the van’s rear doors. Mr Andrulis was arrested the following day on suspicion of possessing a controlled drug with intent to supply. The suspect claimed he was asked to drop the van at the address, and it would then be returned to him hours later with the hot tub removed and denied any knowledge of the drugs. He added he had been asked to make the delivery by a man he knew as ‘Sprite’, the NCA said in a statement issued on Tuesday. The man appeared at Laganside Crown Court in June, before being sentenced to two years and two months in prison on Tuesday, 11 th August. NCA Branch Commander David Cunningham said: “Paulius Andrulis went to great lengths to hide this haul of drugs in his van, with a specialist hide running the length of the roof. PICTURE NCA/PSNI “He denied any knowledge of these drugs but our investigation showed he had likely been involved in a number of previous smuggling runs and his account at interview lacked credibility. “We are grateful to our partners at Border Force who discovered these drugs. The NCA will continue to do all we can to stop drugs being smuggled into Northern Ireland and across the border.” John-Jo Oldham, Assistant Director, Border Force Northern Ireland said: “This expert interception demonstrates that Border Force is relentless in combatting drug smuggling. “These drugs destroy lives, inflicts misery on our communities and fuels further offending. “We continue to work round the clock to pursue criminality, protect the UK’s borders and keep these dangerous drugs off our streets.” Belfast based Phoenix Law holds jailhouse talks with alleged drugs cartel boss Daniel Kinahan Five men arrested as part of £1m drug bust in Belfast Driver who claimed he was delivering hot tub jailed for smuggling cannabis Drugs, dereliction and rough sleepers to greet 800,000 Fleadh visitors, Belfast business owner warns Suspected drugs worth £50,000 recovered in Causeway Coast UPS worker ‘King’ jailed for 12 years over £10m cocaine smuggling operation Most read 1 Country superstar Dolly Parton dies aged 80 2 ‘It’s unbelievable to have Dáithí back in Ballymurphy’ – A new life awaits Belfast boy who changed Northern Ireland’s organ donation law 3 FIFA Council not been told which agency will consider 64-team World Cup impact 4 Man accused of violent tirade in Belfast hospital apologises to judge for saying he wanted him shot dead 5 Class TT hat-trick for Dunlop Top stories 1 John Manley: Sinn Féin may yet feel the heat from John Finucane’s ill-judged meeting with Daniel Kinahan 2 DUP councillor questions PSNI arrest operation connected to replica mosque on loyalist bonfire 3 Sinn Féin sees ‘no justification’ for Drumcree parade as unionists demand Parades Commission members quit 4 Man accused of violent tirade in Belfast hospital apologises to judge for saying he wanted him shot dead 5 Former council chief Anne Donaghy’s ‘dismay’ that email she wanted deleted was ‘upstairs’ points to intent, court told

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text: A tanker collided with a river cruise liner, the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage, carrying 129 passengers plus crew in New Orleans on Friday. The cruise liner was taking on water as it rapidly turned on its side, and videos showed people climbing on to the railing to avoid falling in the water. New Orleans mayor Helena Moreno’s communication team said multiple individuals have been rescued, and search-and-rescue operations remain ongoing. Helicopters were seen in the air along with ambulances waiting nearby. It is currently unclear if there are any fatalities and whether all passengers and crew are out of the water. It is also unclear exactly what caused the collision. A source told the Guardian that it was possible the tanker had lost power before striking the cruise liner. Maritime experts speculated the incident may have been caused by either steerage failure or engine failure. https://www.politico.eu/article/5-ways-e.text: BRUSSELS — The U.S. and Russia are pressing Europe to overhaul the continent’s security architecture in a bid to end the war in Ukraine — and that could mean anything from giving Moscow a bigger say to no change at all. Russian President Vladimir Putin has long insisted on a rethink of European defense, demanding that NATO pull back its forces and that Russia be given a key voice in the continent's security — calls that predate the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But Donald Trump — keen to get a deal to end the war — is now aligning with some of that thinking. Advertisement Advertisement “Security guarantees for Ukraine cannot be finalized in isolation from post-war European security architecture. The two must be considered together,” Trump's peace envoy Jared Kushner wrote Sunday. POLITICO spoke to 12 former and current European officials, experts and NATO diplomats, many of whom were granted anonymity to speak candidly. They laid out clear red lines: no talks without Europe, no unilateral decisions about Ukraine’s NATO accession and no new deal until the war ends. “We have a security order in Europe, we don't have any need of changing that,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said in an interview. Here are five possible scenarios — and POLITICO's assessment of how likely they are to happen. Not all are mutually exclusive. 1. A beefed-up OSCE The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, headquartered in Vienna, is one of the few European security bodies Russia still belongs to. Its Vienna Document lays out risk-reduction measures like asking countries to announce military activities involving 9,000 or more troops at least 42 days in advance. Advertisement Advertisement If there is a peace deal, the OSCE could be a ready-made venue for ceasefire monitoring, finalizing more granular aspects of peace talks and confidence-building measures like new military activity notifications, said Ulrich Kühn, head of the research department for arms control at the IFSH think tank. That comes as over 40 countries in Dublin this month backed “discussions on further risk management and reduction mechanisms that contribute to stability in Europe” in the event of a peace deal. The downside is the 57-member organization’s “cumbersome” size and consensus-oriented decision-making, said Sven Biscop, director of the Europe program at the Egmont Institute. The institution is open to a broader role. “We need to make full use of this unique platform to preserve dialogue, rebuild transparency, reduce risks and manage tensions,” OSCE Secretary-General Feridun Sinirlioğlu told POLITICO. “The OSCE remains a key forum for rebuilding a more stable and predictable security architecture in Europe.” Likelihood: 3/5 Advertisement Advertisement 2. A revived NATO-Russia Council Reviving the moribund NATO-Russia Council is an idea backed by Kushner. Established in 2002 , it was a forum for consultation, risk reduction and joint decision-making — leading to limited agreements like a mutual submarine crew rescue deal and joint counterterrorism plans . The council could make decisions by consensus on its own work, but gave Russia no veto over NATO’s decisions or allied defense policies. It last met a month before Moscow’s full-scale invasion. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has since declared the format is “dead.” The military alliance still maintains a communication line to Russia’s top general, Valery Gerasimov. But that link is largely unused, primarily because Russia refuses to engage, according to one NATO diplomat and one NATO official. When contact does happen, “the content of exchanges is more of parallel monologues,” said the diplomat. Reviving the council after a peace deal could help manage escalation, said two other alliance diplomats. But they cautioned that it should be done carefully, as it could lend Russia legitimacy. Advertisement Advertisement Likelihood: 2/5 3. A new security treaty A sweeping new Europe-wide agreement that builds on today’s institutions — or replaces them wholesale — is another possibility; but it’s also likely to meet the most resistance from Ukraine’s allies. A new pact would have advantages, said Egmont's Biscop. It could bring into play new realities like Finland's and Sweden's membership in NATO and Ukraine’s EU aspirations, as well as new military risks like AI. “The geopolitics have changed … so you can't just restart where you left off — you will have to renegotiate,” he said. Any new treaty also risks fueling European fears over giving Russia too much say over the continent’s security architecture. “There is absolutely no basis for questioning existing alliances. We will not discuss such matters,” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said last week. Advertisement Advertisement Even less palatable for Europe is Russia’s proposal to strike deals with individual NATO nations. “These could be bilateral agreements that … meet the criteria of mutual non-aggression pacts,” Russian foreign ministry policy planning chief Alexey Drobinin said earlier this month. For NATO, that’s a “complete no-go,” said one alliance diplomat, arguing it would allow Moscow to drive wedges between allies. A narrower option is the U.S. suggestion that Ukraine be granted NATO-like security guarantees. But Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov on Friday called it "an option that is unacceptable to us." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also has questions. "When we talk about 'Article 5-like' guarantees, we need answers to some very clear questions. Which countries will support Ukraine if Ukraine is attacked again? What exactly will our partners do in response? Which troops will be stationed on our territory in advance? How much will all this cost? And will it really work?" Zelenskyy told the NATO Parliamentary Assembly on Monday. Advertisement Likelihood: 1/5 4. A fresh EU-Russia format The EU, too, once had a formal cooperation channel with Russia under the 1997 Partnership and Cooperation Agreement . The Permanent Partnership Council convened ministerial meetings on external security, justice, research and economic issues and led to agreements on visa facilitation and border cooperation . It was frozen after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014. The EU’s mandate in issues like trade, sanctions, visas and border management gives it flexibility and leverage with Moscow in establishing post-war relations, said one EU diplomat, while stressing that the bloc has a limited mandate on security issues. “As long as such a format is perceived as an alteration of the current security architecture in Europe, it will not fly,” the diplomat said. “It will need to be framed as an annex to the current architecture.” Any bid to normalize economic and energy ties with Russia carries risks, added Kühn. Advertisement “You don't want to go full speed and let the Russian gas flow again because you make yourself very vulnerable,” he said. “This will take some time … confidence [and] security-building measures come first.” And it won't just be Brussels alone talking to Moscow. “Any meaningful discussions about Europe's security framework can only be undertaken once a ceasefire in Ukraine has been achieved ... in particular with NATO allies and EU members,” said a European Commission spokesperson. Likelihood: 2/5 5. Everything stays the same Officials say this is the likeliest option — even as Moscow makes clear this is unacceptable. In part, that’s because Europe’s most important military and economic alliances have never included Russia, said Biscop. Advertisement “There's just one EU and one NATO of which Russia cannot be a member, so this means geopolitically, Russia is now a neighbor of Europe,” he said. “We’re never going to devise a sort of security architecture that allows us to co-decide.” “It's not a good scenario … it will be very unstable,” said Biscop, but “given the unrealistic Russian demands, it's quite likely that this is where we end up.” The same NATO diplomat cited above put it more bluntly. “Russia has completely disregarded any peace agreements agreed upon in the past 30 years,” they said. “If you want to rebuild a conversation, you need to have both people agreeing on its terms, you can’t have just one — that’s talking to yourself.” Likelihood: 4/5
